questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a complete sulcus?
questions.explanation: The collateral sulcus is a complete sulcus. A complete sulcus is deep enough to indent the wall of a ventricle. The posterior part of the calcarine sulcus is an axial sulcus, while the anterior part is a complete sulcus. Therefore, among the options provided, the collateral sulcus is the best answer.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Anterior part of the calcarine sulcus is a _______.
questions.explanation: The anterior part of the calcarine sulcus is considered a complete sulcus because its depth creates an elevation in the medial wall of the occipital horn of the lateral ventricle called the calcar avis. The posterior part of the calcarine sulcus is considered an axial sulcus because its axis lies along the visual cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Where is Heschl's gyrus located?
questions.explanation: Heschl's gyrus is located in the primary auditory cortex, corresponding to Brodmann areas 41 and 42.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true?

options.text: Area marked A is Broca's area (44, 45) and is present in the inferior frontal gyrus
Area marked B is the visual association area (17, 18) and is present around the calcarine sulcus
Area marked C is the motor association area (5, 7) and is found in the superior parietal lobule
Area marked D is the frontal eye field (8) and is found in the middle frontal gyrus

questions.correctAnswerText: Area marked D is the frontal eye field (8) and is found in the middle frontal gyrus
questions.explanation: Area marked D is the frontal eye field (Brodmann area 8), located in the posterior part of the middle frontal gyrus. It controls conjugate movements of the eyes and is connected to the visual part of the occipital cortex. Lesions here cause loss of horizontal conjugate movements. The source also summarizes important cortical functional areas, including Wernicke's area (22), Broca's area (44,45), visual association cortex (18,19), primary visual cortex (17), and sensory association cortex (5,7).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with inability to form words but can make noises. He also knows what he wants to say. What area of the brain has been damaged in this patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of Broca's aphasia, in which Broca's area is affected. In Broca's aphasia (motor/non-fluent aphasia), Brodmann areas 44 and 45 in the prefrontal and premotor facial regions of the cerebral cortex are affected. Patients have difficulty forming verbal or written words. Comprehension is preserved, but the person cannot repeat or name words normally and lacks fluency. Severe involvement may leave the patient with very few words to express emotions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: In individuals with a history of substance abuse and addiction, the marked structure is believed to trigger cravings on exposure to environmental cues. Which of the following is not true about the structure?

options.text: It forms the base of the sylvian cistern
It lies between the frontal and temporal lobe
It receives somatosensory inputs from the entire body

questions.explanation: The marked structure is the insular lobe. The insular cortex is not entirely agranular: its posterior part is granular and its anterior part is agranular. The insula forms the base of the Sylvian cistern, lies between the frontal and temporal lobes, and receives somatosensory, viscerosensory, homeostatic and nociceptive information from the entire body, including inputs from the thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 72-year-old man presents with a speech abnormality following a hemorrhagic stroke. He does not understand any written words or conversation. His speech is fluent but incomprehensible. Repetition is also impaired. Where is the lesion located?
questions.explanation: Comprehension and repetition are impaired while fluency is intact, pointing to Wernicke's aphasia. Wernicke's area is located in the superior temporal gyrus and is marked as 4 in the source diagram. Broca's motor speech area (44,45) is located in the inferior frontal gyrus.
